This can be formalized as a two-stage decision problem: first, the sacrificial impact creates a state where the team-mate has a higher probability $p$ of scoring; second, the agent's utility function trades off the risk of failure against the certainty of personal justification. Mathematically, the player maximizes $U = p \cdot V_{\text{victory}} - (1-p) \cdot C_{\text{failure}}$, where $V_{\text{victory}}$ is the value of winning and $C_{\text{failure}}$ is the cost of being blamed. In GSE, this maps to a state-transition kernel where the sacrificial action shifts the ball carrier's position distribution toward the goal line. In GSI, the same principle underlies conformal prediction: the player's 'attempt' serves as a valid null hypothesis that cannot be rejected by the crowd's collective judgment, thus preserving the posterior credibility interval.

reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: This reasoning traces back to von Neumann's minimax theorem (1928), which introduced the concept of optimal mixed strategies under uncertainty. It also draws from Arrow's impossibility theorem (1951) in social choice theory, explaining why individual sacrifice can be socially justified even when outcomes are random. The idea of 'justifiable failure' echoes Kelly's bettor (1956), who showed that maximizing log wealth leads to strategies that are never regretted ex-post.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: Opposing agents include the defender, who calculates the probability of preventing the touchdown based on the attacker's momentum; the quarterback, who assesses whether the block opens a passing lane; and the crowd, whose collective cheering acts as a noisy signal of the play's success. Each actor updates their beliefs conditional on the sacrificial impact's outcome.
